title: Energy, bonds and ATP
goal: Explain how energy held in fuel molecules reaches muscle work through ATP, what a coupled reaction is, and why ATP is a carrier rather than a store.

steps.title: Energy is held in chemical bonds
steps.text:
A molecule is atoms held together by chemical bonds. Bonds hold energy. When a big fuel molecule such as glucose or a fatty acid is broken down to carbon dioxide and water, the products hold less energy than the fuel did, and the difference is released.

Cells run two kinds of chemistry:

- [Catabolism](g:catabolism): breaking fuels down, which **releases** energy.
- [Anabolism](g:anabolism): building molecules (glycogen, proteins, new mitochondria), which **needs** energy.

[ATP](g:atp) is the go-between that links the two [[c:atp-link]]. Fuel breakdown is used to rebuild ATP; ATP is then spent on contraction, pumping and building. Because the muscle's ATP pool is small, those pathways must keep running to resupply it [[c:atp-resupply]].

claims.text: ATP is the energy exchange factor that connects catabolism and anabolism, and it fuels contraction, phosphorylation and active transport.

evidence.quote: ATP is universally seen as the energy exchange factor that connects anabolism and catabolism but also fuels processes such as motile contraction, phosphorylations, and active transport.

claims.text: Because muscle ATP stores are small, metabolic pathways fed by carbohydrate and fat must keep resynthesising ATP.

evidence.quote: Because the muscle stores of ATP are small, metabolic pathways must be activated to maintain the required rates of ATP resynthesis.

steps.title: Coupled reactions: paying for uphill jobs
steps.text:
Many jobs in a cell are uphill: they would never happen on their own. Pushing sodium out of a fibre when far more of it is already outside, or joining glucose units into glycogen, are examples.

The cell does them with a [coupled reaction](g:coupled-reaction): it links the uphill job to a downhill one that releases more energy, almost always ATP [hydrolysis](g:hydrolysis) (ATP → [ADP](g:adp) + phosphate). Together, the pair runs downhill.

A clear example is the [sodium–potassium pump](g:na-k-atpase): each ATP it splits moves 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in, both against their gradients [[c:pump-coupling]].

No coupling is perfect. The energy that isn't turned into work appears as **heat** [[c:heat]]: the reason you warm up within minutes of starting to run.

claims.text: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase uses the energy from hydrolysing one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in.

evidence.quote: The active transport of these cations is mediated by the Na+-K+-ATPase, an integral membrane protein that uses the energy from the hydrolysis of 1 ATP to transport 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ into the cell.

claims.text: Muscles convert energy from ATP into work; the energy not converted into work appears as heat.

evidence.quote: Muscles convert energy from ATP into useful work, which can be used to move limbs and to transport ions across membranes.
The energy not converted into work appears as heat.

steps.title: How much energy is in one ATP?
steps.text:
In a working muscle, splitting one ATP releases about **100 zJ** (zeptojoules; 1 zJ = 10⁻²¹ J) [[c:atp-100zj]]. That is tiny, so chemists count per **mole**: 6.02 × 10²³ molecules. Per mole it comes to about 60 kJ.

The myosin [cross-bridge](g:cross-bridge) can turn at most about 50 zJ of each ATP into work, so even the motor itself is at best about 50% efficient [[c:xb-efficiency]]. The rest becomes heat.

The whole body loses more on the way (pumps, breathing, the heart, rebuilding ATP from food), which is why a cyclist's gross efficiency is far below 50%, as the units module showed.

claims.text: Each ATP molecule provides about 100 zJ of energy that can potentially be converted into work.

evidence.quote: Each ATP molecule provides 100 zJ of energy that can potentially be converted into work.

claims.text: A cross-bridge can do at most about 50 zJ of work per ATP, so its maximum efficiency is about 50%.

evidence.quote: The mechanics of the myosin cross-bridge are such that at most 50 zJ of work can be done in one ATP consuming cycle; that is, the maximum efficiency of a cross-bridge is ∼50%.

steps.title: From one molecule to a mole
steps.problem: One ATP releases 100 zJ when split. How much energy is that per mole of ATP (6.02 × 10²³ molecules)?
steps: Write the prefix as a power of ten: 100 zJ = 100 × 10⁻²¹ J = 1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Energy per mole = energy per molecule × molecules per mole = 1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Multiply the numbers and add the powers: 6.02 × 10⁴ J·mol⁻¹ = 60,200 J·mol⁻¹ ≈ 60 kJ·mol⁻¹.
Check the size: one molecule is tiny, a mole is huge, so the answer should land in the everyday range of kJ. It does.

steps.title: ATP is a carrier, not a store
steps.text:
ATP is recycled, not hoarded. Even at rest, each muscle cell holds about a billion ATP molecules, and all of them are used and replaced about every 2 minutes. In hard exercise, ATP production can rise about 1,000-fold [[c:atp-turnover]].

So think of ATP as a rechargeable battery that is drained and recharged nonstop, while the real fuel tanks are glycogen and fat. Resting before a race can't "fill up" your ATP; it can fill up glycogen.

How muscle recharges ATP fast enough (phosphocreatine, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation) is the subject of the bioenergetics module. Here, the key idea is simpler: fuel energy → ATP → work and heat.

claims.text: Each muscle cell holds about a billion ATP molecules, all used and replaced about every 2 minutes at rest; ATP production can rise 1,000-fold in intense exercise.

evidence.quote: Even at rest, each muscle cell contains roughly 1 billion ATP molecules, all of which will be used and replaced every 2 minutes; during intense exercise, muscle ATP production can increase 1000-fold to meet the demands of intense muscle contraction.

points: Fuel molecules hold energy in their bonds; breaking them down (catabolism) releases it, building molecules (anabolism) needs it.
ATP links the two: fuel breakdown rebuilds ATP, and ATP hydrolysis pays for contraction, pumping and building.
Uphill jobs are coupled to ATP hydrolysis, e.g. 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP; energy not turned into work becomes heat.
One ATP gives about 100 zJ (about 60 kJ·mol⁻¹); a cross-bridge is at best about 50% efficient.
ATP is a carrier recycled every few minutes even at rest; the stores are glycogen and fat.

variants.stem: Which description best fits ATP's role in a cell?

options.text: A carrier passing energy from fuel to work
options.why: Right: ATP links catabolism (which rebuilds it) to contraction, pumping and building (which spend it).

options.text: The cell's long-term store of energy
options.why: ATP is recycled within minutes; long-term energy is stored as glycogen and fat.

options.text: A fuel the cell takes in from food
options.why: Food supplies carbohydrate, fat and protein; the cell makes its own ATP from them.

options.text: An enzyme that speeds up fuel breakdown
options.why: ATP is a substrate and energy carrier, not an enzyme.

variants.stem: During a long run, energy from fat and glycogen ends up moving the legs. What role does ATP play in that chain?

options.text: The go-between: fuel breakdown rebuilds ATP, and ATP powers contraction
options.why: Right: ATP connects energy-releasing and energy-using reactions.

options.text: A by-product made after contraction is done
options.why: ATP is spent during contraction, not made after it.

options.text: A backup fuel used only when glycogen runs out
options.why: ATP is used every moment of every contraction, not as a backup.

options.text: A store that is filled before the run and drained during it
options.why: The ATP pool is tiny and recycled nonstop; it can't be filled up in advance.

variants.stem: After a hard ride, a cyclist's muscles rebuild glycogen from glucose. What kind of process is this?

options.text: Anabolism, which needs energy from ATP
options.why: Right: building a big molecule from small ones is anabolism and costs energy.
Catabolism breaks molecules down; making glycogen builds one up.
Building molecules needs energy; it doesn't release it.

options.text: Catabolism, which needs energy from ATP
options.why: Catabolism is the breaking-down side, and overall it releases energy.

variants.stem: A runner's leg fibres keep Na⁺ low inside even though Na⁺ leaks in with every nerve signal. How can the fibre push Na⁺ out, against its gradient?

options.text: By coupling the transport to ATP hydrolysis in the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
options.why: Right: each ATP split moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the pair of reactions runs downhill together.

options.text: By diffusion, which moves Na⁺ out on its own
options.why: Diffusion only moves Na⁺ down its gradient, which is into the fibre.

options.text: By using heat released from contraction
options.why: Heat can't be harnessed to drive pumps; it is the lost part of the energy.

options.text: By using oxygen directly to push the ions out
options.why: Oxygen is used in mitochondria to rebuild ATP; the pump itself runs on ATP.

variants.stem: Ten minutes into a hard turbo session indoors, a cyclist's core temperature is rising fast even though the room is cool. What is the main source of this heat?

options.text: Energy from ATP and fuel breakdown that is not turned into work
options.why: Right: no coupling is perfect, and the energy not converted into work appears as heat.

options.text: Friction between the legs and the bike
options.why: Friction in the drivetrain warms the bike, not the body; the heat comes from the muscles.

options.text: Heat absorbed from the room air
options.why: The room is cool; the body is losing heat to the air, not gaining it.

options.text: Heat released by the heart pumping blood
options.why: The heart produces some heat, but the working leg muscles produce far more.

variants.stem: Splitting one ATP releases 100 zJ (1 zJ = 10⁻²¹ J). A mole holds 6.02 × 10²³ molecules. About how much energy is released per mole of ATP?

options.why: Right: 1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 6.02 × 10⁴ J·mol⁻¹ ≈ 60 kJ·mol⁻¹.
This takes 100 zJ as 10⁻²⁰ J (one power of ten lost).
This takes 100 zJ as 10⁻¹⁸ J (one power of ten too many).
This divides by the number of molecules instead of multiplying.

variants.solution: 100 zJ = 100 × 10⁻²¹ J = 10⁻¹⁹ J. Per mole: 10⁻¹⁹ J × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 6.02 × 10⁴ J·mol⁻¹ ≈ 60 kJ·mol⁻¹.

variants.stem: Splitting one ATP releases 100 zJ (1 zJ = 10⁻²¹ J). How many ATP must be split to release 1 J?

options.why: Right: 1 J ÷ 10⁻¹⁹ J per ATP = 10¹⁹ ATP.
This forgets the 100 in 100 zJ: 1 ÷ 10⁻²¹.
This takes zepto as 10⁻¹⁹ instead of 10⁻²¹, so 100 zJ becomes 10⁻¹⁷ J and the count comes out 100 times too small.
That is the number in a mole, which releases about 60 kJ, not 1 J.

variants.solution: 100 zJ = 10⁻¹⁹ J. Number of ATP = 1 J ÷ 10⁻¹⁹ J = 10¹⁹ ATP (about 17 millionths of a mole).

variants.stem: In a sprint, a muscle sample splits 1 mmol of ATP. Each mole of ATP releases about 60 kJ. How much energy is released?

options.why: Right: 0.001 mol × 60 kJ·mol⁻¹ = 0.06 kJ = 60 J.
This forgets the milli: 1 mmol is 0.001 mol.
This applies the milli twice: 0.06 kJ is 60 J, not 0.06 J.
This slips one power of ten, e.g. taking 1 mmol as 10⁻⁴ mol. 1 mmol = 10⁻³ mol, so 10⁻³ × 60,000 J = 60 J.

variants.solution: 1 mmol = 10⁻³ mol. Energy = 10⁻³ mol × 60 kJ·mol⁻¹ = 0.06 kJ = 60 J.

variants.stem: A cross-bridge cycle splits one ATP (100 zJ) and does 40 zJ of work. What is its efficiency, and how much energy becomes heat?

options.why: Right: efficiency = work ÷ energy in = 40 ÷ 100 = 40%; the other 60 zJ is heat.
This swaps work and heat: 60 zJ is the heat, not the work.
This divides energy in by work (100 ÷ 40). Efficiency can't exceed 100%.
Energy isn't lost: what isn't work appears as heat (100 − 40 = 60 zJ).

variants.solution: Efficiency = work ÷ energy in = 40 zJ ÷ 100 zJ = 0.40 = 40%. Heat = 100 − 40 = 60 zJ.

variants.stem: A cross-bridge cycle splits one ATP (100 zJ) and does 30 zJ of work. What is its efficiency, and how much energy becomes heat?

options.why: Right: 30 ÷ 100 = 30%; the other 70 zJ is heat.
This swaps work and heat.
This divides energy in by work (100 ÷ 30). Efficiency can't exceed 100%.
What isn't work appears as heat: 100 − 30 = 70 zJ.

variants.stem: A cross-bridge cycle splits one ATP (100 zJ) and does 45 zJ of work. What is its efficiency, and how much energy becomes heat?

options.why: Right: 45 ÷ 100 = 45%; the other 55 zJ is heat. Close to the ~50% ceiling.
This swaps work and heat.
This divides energy in by work (100 ÷ 45). Efficiency can't exceed 100%.
What isn't work appears as heat: 100 − 45 = 55 zJ.

variants.stem: A triathlete says: "I rest completely the day before a race to top up my ATP stores." What is the best judgement?

options.text: Wrong idea: ATP is recycled within minutes; rest tops up glycogen
options.why: Right: the ATP pool is tiny and replaced about every 2 minutes even at rest; the stores that a rest day refills are glycogen.

options.text: Right: ATP builds up over a rest day for use in the race
options.why: ATP can't be stockpiled; it is used and replaced every few minutes.

options.text: Right: ATP is the body's main long-term energy store
options.why: The long-term stores are glycogen and fat; ATP is the carrier.

options.text: Wrong idea: muscles don't use ATP during races
options.why: Muscles use ATP for every contraction; the error is thinking it can be stored up.
